title: Saudi Arabia Quietly Flags UAE as High-Risk for Financial Transfers
excerpt: The kingdom has placed UAE-bound bank transfers under enhanced anti-money-laundering scrutiny, disrupting payments for businesses and individuals — including millions of Indian expats in the Gulf.
body:
• Saudi Arabia's central bank has instructed banks to apply enhanced due diligence on financial transfers to the UAE, placing it alongside countries like Lebanon and Iraq on a high-risk list for financial crimes.
  • Multiple businesses and individuals report transfers being delayed for weeks or returned without explanation, with some rerouting payments through third countries.
  • Sources describe the measures as a "subtle message" amid escalating Saudi-UAE tensions over OPEC, Yemen, and economic competition — with direct implications for millions of Indian workers who remit money through Gulf banking corridors.

Saudi Arabia has quietly placed financial transfers to the United Arab Emirates under extra layers of regulatory scrutiny normally reserved for countries considered high-risk for money laundering and terrorism financing, according to Reuters, citing three people with direct knowledge of the matter.

The previously unreported measures have disrupted cross-border payments between the Gulf's two largest economies. Six businesspeople told Reuters their companies have had transfers in various currencies delayed or returned by Saudi banks with no official explanation.

What Changed

Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia's central bank — known as SAMA — notified key banks to apply enhanced due diligence when handling settlements with the UAE, the sources said. The additional checks place the UAE among more than half a dozen countries in the region deemed high-risk, alongside Lebanon, South Sudan, and Iraq — all of which sit on the Financial Action Task Force's "grey list" of jurisdictions requiring additional monitoring.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2089662369718788459

The classification is notable because the FATF only delisted the UAE in 2024 after it made improvements to its anti-money-laundering regime, a decision some anti-corruption groups argued was premature.

SAMA denied imposing targeted restrictions. "There are no direct restrictions on specific countries," the central bank said, adding that banks apply "necessary controls and preventive measures to mitigate risks based on their own internal assessments."

A UAE official similarly said the economy ministry had not received reports of unusual difficulties, and emphasized that the two countries "maintain deep and longstanding economic and commercial ties."

Impact on the Ground

The gap between official statements and lived experience is wide. Three bankers told Reuters that enhanced oversight means transfers to the UAE now pass through more compliance checks. Some take weeks to clear; others never make it through at all.

"Some Saudi clients were struggling to make payments and had advised him to set up operations elsewhere."

— Head of a Dubai-based consultancy, as reported by Reuters

Three businesspeople said their firms now route payments through third countries to bypass the bottleneck. In one reported case, a Dubai-based service provider and a Saudi client abandoned traditional banking channels entirely and completed a transaction through PayPal despite the additional costs.

The disruptions began in the weeks after the UAE announced on April 28 that it was leaving OPEC, the oil-producing group effectively led by Saudi Arabia — a move widely seen as a direct challenge to Riyadh's influence.

A Wider Gulf Rift

A Saudi insider told Reuters the enhanced oversight was intended as a "subtle message" to Emirati leaders about the importance of maintaining good relations. Four regional financial-sector sources shared this interpretation.

The two monarchies were once among the closest allies in the Arab world, but their relationship has deteriorated amid competing visions for the post-oil economy, disagreements over Yemen — where Saudi Arabia accused the UAE of backing secessionist forces — and divergent responses to the Iran conflict.

While Dubai remains the Gulf's dominant business hub, Saudi Arabia has aggressively pushed multinational companies to relocate regional headquarters to Riyadh, making it a condition to win large government contracts. The economic competition adds a structural dimension to what were once mainly diplomatic disputes.

Analysts caution that a full economic rupture is unlikely given the depth of Saudi-UAE trade — the kingdom is the UAE's largest Arab trading partner — but the financial squeeze signals that Riyadh is willing to use economic levers to assert its position.

What This Means for Indian Expats

The disruptions carry direct consequences for millions of Indian workers in the Gulf. India is the top source of remittances globally, with the UAE and Saudi Arabia ranking among the largest corridors. Indians in Saudi Arabia who send money to family or business accounts in the UAE — or who work for companies that transact between the two countries — may face unexpected delays.

The situation also matters for Indian businesses with operations across both countries. Trade and services firms that rely on smooth Saudi-UAE financial flows could see working capital squeezed if the enhanced oversight persists.

What to Watch

Neither government has acknowledged a political dimension to the financial measures. But with OPEC dynamics shifting, Yemen tensions unresolved, and economic competition intensifying, the Saudi-UAE corridor bears watching. For now, businesses and individuals caught in the middle are adapting — rerouting payments, switching platforms, and waiting.
